title: REST vs gRPC Decision Framework
description: Learn when to choose REST over gRPC for C# service communication, and when the performance and contract benefits of gRPC justify its operational costs.

data.text: REST and gRPC are the two dominant service communication styles in the .NET ecosystem. REST uses HTTP with JSON, is human-readable, and works everywhere. gRPC uses HTTP/2 with Protocol Buffers, is binary and efficient, and provides strong contracts through .proto files. Both are excellent. The senior engineer's choice depends on the communication pattern: internal high-volume service calls favor gRPC, while public APIs and browser clients favor REST.

A common mistake is choosing gRPC because it is 'modern' or faster, without considering whether the application actually needs binary efficiency or streaming. A CRUD API with low traffic and simple data shapes gains nothing from gRPC and loses browser compatibility, debugging simplicity, and the vast ecosystem of HTTP tooling. Conversely, a data pipeline moving millions of records between internal services benefits enormously from gRPC's binary format and bidirectional streaming.

data.title: Use REST when
items: The API is public-facing and consumed by browsers, mobile apps, or third-party integrators.
Team familiarity with HTTP and JSON is high, and learning gRPC would slow delivery.
Payload size and latency are within acceptable ranges for JSON over HTTP.
You need broad tooling support: API gateways, monitoring, and client generators.
The communication pattern is simple request-response without streaming.

data.title: Use gRPC when
items: Services communicate internally with high throughput and low latency requirements.
You need streaming: real-time data feeds, chat, or live telemetry.
Strong contracts between services are important for versioning and compatibility.
Payload efficiency matters: mobile networks, IoT devices, or high-frequency trading.
The team has experience with Protocol Buffers or the time to learn them.

data.title: gRPC is not free
data.text: gRPC requires HTTP/2, TLS configuration, and specialized tooling for debugging. In Kubernetes, you may need a gRPC-aware ingress controller. For browser clients, you need gRPC-Web with a proxy like Envoy. These are solvable problems, but they are costs that must be included in the decision.

A gRPC service in C# is defined by a .proto file and a generated service class. The contract is explicit, the serialization is fast, and the client libraries are generated automatically for multiple languages.

items.text: Are the clients web browsers or mobile apps that need broad compatibility?
items.hint: If yes, REST is the safer default.

items.text: Is the communication internal between services with high throughput?
items.hint: If yes, gRPC likely provides better performance.

items.text: Do you need streaming data (server-to-client or bidirectional)?
items.hint: If yes, gRPC is purpose-built for streaming.

items.text: Is the team comfortable with Protocol Buffers and HTTP/2 debugging tools?
items.hint: If no, REST reduces operational risk.

items.text: Are you deploying to an environment where gRPC is fully supported (ingress, service mesh, monitoring)?
items.hint: If no, REST avoids infrastructure complications.

data.title: Choose REST or gRPC for your service
data.description: Apply the decision framework to a real service in your project or a hypothetical scenario.
steps: Identify a service that needs an API: public-facing or internal.
List the clients: browsers, mobile apps, other services, third-party integrators.
Estimate throughput: how many requests per second, and what is the acceptable latency?
Determine if streaming is required for any interaction.
Assess the team's gRPC experience and the infrastructure's gRPC support.
Make a recommendation: REST, gRPC, or a hybrid. Write your trade-off statement.
data.expectedOutcome: A justified REST vs gRPC decision with a written trade-off statement.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: REST is simpler, more compatible, and better for public-facing or browser-consumed APIs.
gRPC is faster, more efficient, and better for internal high-volume service communication.
gRPC requires HTTP/2, Protocol Buffers, and specialized infrastructure support.
The choice should be based on client needs, throughput, streaming requirements, and team maturity.
data.takeaway: Both REST and gRPC are excellent tools. Senior engineers choose the one that fits the problem context, not the one that is fashionable or familiar.
